subject: RMF-30 Zoning
comment: Our neighborhood recently held a community meeting to discuss the Salt Lake City Planning Commission's "Affordable Housing Incentives" proposal document. I believe this is how different parties talking about the same issue. A realtor from the neighborhood verified that the average sales price for the area specifically addressed in the Planning Commission document for a single-family home in the last 180 days was $551,000. I understand that on face value, this is an expensive area. However, to be replaced by the proposed development of 12-20 units to make a profit, the builder would need to save wherever possible -- likely in materials and workmanship. It is unlikely that the new construction would "fit in" with the historical homes. On the other hand, I look at the thousands of homes being built on the west side of Salt Lake City and note that while the structures are impressive, they create 17-newer high-rise buildings with at least 3 rows to count that are in planning or construction stages and understand that the number of affordable units there are dwarfed. The chairman of the last use and zoning committee indicated that up zoning proposals such as the one in our neighborhood are happening because it's "Smart? Certainly a missed opportunity. The need is there, but allowing a zeros on existing lots in frightening. The homes in this area were built in the early 1900s. Mine is a "newer" home for that area and was built in 1939. These homes have stood for over 100 years and are historical and bring significant charm to the area. They were all built with a 20% frontage. The only way a 3-5 lot lot could accommodate 4-6 units is to demolish the existing historical home and built vertically lot size to lot line. I pity the next-door neighbors. They would likely not see sunlight at all during a significant part of the day. I also fear there would be significant noise impact on the surrounding neighborhood is also known for an abundance of older large trees. I assume all but those on the park strip would need to be removed to accommodate the larger buildings. I thought Mayor Mendenhall's goal was to increase the tree canopy not eliminate it. I'm also concerned about the impact of additional population density on the area. As a "city worker" I spoke with told me the pipes are pretty much rusted away and you can see the sewage as it moves through the disintegrating pipes. Who will pay for the repairs or replacement needed to accommodate the increased usage? In addition, I might mention that the power in our area goes out regularly during storms (and our power block was without power for 4 days. Our power lines are above ground and quite old. Do they have capacity for these increases? Parking on street old, existing streets is also an issue. I have seen the snow plows get stuck because parked cars block the street and prevent clearing. Before my husband and I retire, I need to find street parking no matter what the regulations are. Many don't conform to parking restrictions now. I recommend you target new construction on infill sites rather than demolishing a perfectly good but historic home or an area with more capacity and need such as the west side of Salt Lake City. Please preserve our historical homes and City area.

subject: Proposed Changes to RMF-30 Zoning District
topic: RMF-30 Zoning and Related Development Issues in Salt Lake City
comment: Thank you for the recent mailings reaching out to Salt Lake City residents regarding local housing issues and the resulting to the revised zoning requirements. I am responding to the recent amendment to the city's proposed residential zoning outlined in the 24 July 2019 Staff Report and amended 25 September 2019 report. While I agree in principle with the amendments/effects I am against the proposed changes as the unintended consequences of these revisions will unnecessarily concentrate affordable housing in areas that also need improvements within current communities, infrastructure, and employment. Local Historic Districts, and more specifically to the Central City area from 400 South to Liberty Park between 500 and 700 East, I believe this is a prime example of what remains of a quintessential historic Salt Lake City residential neighborhood that is in need of preservation. Much of what has built in that area is in the 1800s and early 1900s. After the subdivision based on the southwestern edge of Liberty Park. Considering the intense development that has taken place in downtown, the largest destruction of historical structures, loss of green space, and the huge, haphazard apartment complexes already built around what used to be a low rise residential area. I support that from many concerned residents an effort to limit the rampant growth that has taken place. The Planning Commission and City Council need to take a step back from about 5-year plans and look 20 to 50 years into the future to try and understand what this type of development will have on the well being of the city. A recent survey by the U of U study and the Kem Gardner Institute released in February 2021 and titled "What do residents think?" contains and itemizes both residents surveyed throughout the city felt that it is necessary to maximize profit, without regard to community and adjacent property impacts. Each development should be considered on a case-by-case basis with input from the Historic Landmark Commission, neighboring property owners, local businesses, and other relevant groups. I think everyone would agree that most residents would like improvements for loss of parking strips and reduced open space to a bare minimum, in the area mentioned above the historic residences have maintained large yards, mature trees in the lots as well as the parking strips and center medians and will continue to do so if they are allowed. Historic zoning protection should be, but hasn't been applied to maintain the high standard of quality in the region. With the large number of new apartments complexes along 400 South and in this Liberty Park vicinity, plus the ones about to presume "walkability" undermining the historical integrity and lived organization isn't such as those from trolley systems, the quality of life has already been compromised. Looking to the future with so many new and large multi unit apartment for the park and nearby businesses. Destruction of historical structures. Despite the included incentives for developers to construct affordable housing structures into new development is a highly unlikely this will happen. The options developers have from on-site affordable housing to-off site construction, and in lieu fee are designed to make a profit that allow and not the result of providing affordable housing that is desperately needed. As a city planning consultant, I find this level of ownership. Everywhere you look in this city, beautiful, viable historic structures have been demolished in the name of expediency, profitability and tax base. Historical structures tell what provide a city with character and, more important, lasting value.

subject: Proposed Changes to RMF-30 Zoning District
topic: RMF-30 Zoning and Related Development Issues in Salt Lake City
comment: As pointed out in the reviews, set unit parking requirements present a very real problem for multi-unit and cottage type developments. The reduction of requirements from two to one space for all street parking will very much impact area residents who are walking to access local facilities, and the "walkability" of the neighborhood. Everyone in the city has seen what the unregulated building boom does to neighborhoods and the residents. the need new affordable housing, I think we can all agree, but have any vehicle and that the majority of persons will want to walk or use public transport, this is just not borne out in the daily observations of area citizens moving about. Affordability, as pointed out in the staff reports these zoning changes are not likely to provide substantial affordable units. Rather, these changes are more likely to provide another avenue for developers to take advantage of regulatory changes at the expense of the residents of long-established neighborhoods. Considering the cost of land acquisition and the workplace cost of materials brought on by supply chain issues and demand, developers are categorically unable to provide "affordable housing" again, their objective is to find opportunities and maximize profits. From the perspective of both a resident and a housing advocate, I think we need to realize that historic neighborhood is the most likely alternative with small multi residences and homeowners offering single and multiple family jobs, for rent. If the city wants to preserve the character, and at the same time support affordability, they would do more better to support local people wishing to live in existing structures and provide employment opportunities. I'd like to recommend that the Planning Division Community & Neighborhoods staff, the Planning Commission, the City Council, and Mayor in dealing with a frightening preparation does not mean that identification and zoning of all areas of the city is appropriate Any planners should understand that development is a powerful force that can create both functional and dysfunctional features in a community. Given the history of this city, they will provide a highly desirable real estate market for those young families who move here, live in one of two high apartment complexes, wish to remain and transition to a home that provides a yard in which their children can grow into productive citizens. Those people will likely abandon the community or languish and be unhappy in insufficient housing. Text amendments should not be adopted at this time as Land-anchor change or zoning requirements will adversely open all areas in need of preservation to the long-term destruction and development of existing neighborhoods. However, a number of areas do need increased levels of housing density and these can be addressed through specific zoning changes and design requirements. Ability to construct, side oriented one houses and cottage developments, Limits to maximum lot width, and incentives for retention of historic structures. We not move proposed changes in a project by project basis, while long-term human values and the success of historic elements should be the overriding consideration. This is more important than short-term finance gain.

subject: FW: [EXTERNAL] Re: City budget has doubled in the last 10 years
comment: By way of further elaboration, how does this budget reflect recent realities: a pandemic, a slowdown or temporary stoppage of some city services over the past 3 years, a 40-year high inflation rate that is hitting everyone's pocketbook — especially families and those on fixed incomes, and a decline in school enrollment? You are the guardians of our precious tax dollars. Utah and SLC probably hasn't suffered as much as other capital cities and states, which is fortunate. In fact statistics that SLC had strong post-COVID recovery. But we also don't have the economic foundation that a lot of other states have either. Regarding population, you can even go back in time when Salt Lake City's population was 189,454 in 1960 — 60 years ago. (Source: SLC Mayor's fiscal budget 2011-2012.) It's changed very little yet the city's budget keeps growing exponentially. Understandably, there are many more complexities today than there were in 1960, the cost of just about everything is much higher and the racial composition of the city has changed as well. It would be instructive to know where the greatest demands on city services are and which of those services have grown the most in the last 10 years. If my figures are correct, the city's budget was $330 million in 2019-20, $326 million 2020-21, $349 million 2021-22, and now the "Great Leap Forward" to $424 million in 2022-23. Best, Jan Dan and Tim: Luke Garrott's news article about the mayor's new budget will be a discussion item at Thursday's YNC meeting. Can you also come prepared to talk about the $4 million increase in the Library budget. It appears from the CC work session discussion, our libraries are dealing more and more with the homeless as well as drug and mental health issues. Can we have a fuller disclosure about what they are encountering? In the past 10 years, the SLC budget has doubled while the population has grown 7%. subject: Native Plants Program & Monarch Waystations
comment: Providing habitat for an endangered species in our city parks may seem like a small & trivial thing to some, but it's reflective of the new reality we are facing. As SLC continues to plan for growth and faces drought and water shortages, how we choose to landscape our yards, our parks, new developments and city green spaces is a pivotal part of the master plan. As we face drought and climate change, it is important for people to see examples of landscaping that incorporates water-wise native plants that support wildlife habitat, like the endangered Monarch butterfly, in our parks and public spaces. Please consider funding and expansion of the Monarch Waystation site now thriving in Stansbury Park to new locations in other parks and city green spaces. Through funding and expanding this program, the city can lead by example and raise awareness at this pivotal and crucial time in our state's history.
